blocks.text:
Design a stock exchange, the system that accepts buy and sell orders for a set of tradable symbols and matches them against each other fairly, at extremely low latency, to produce trades. This category's two prior problems both centered on a ledger, a durable record of money that already knows exactly where every unit belongs. This problem is different in kind: the hard part is not recording a known outcome, it is deciding the outcome itself, which two orders trade, at what price, in what order, fairly and deterministically, all while under a latency budget measured in microseconds rather than seconds.

The technique that makes fair, low-latency matching possible is price-time priority over an in-memory order book, the best price always trades first, and among orders at an equal price, whoever arrived first trades first, combined with a durable write-ahead log that lets a crashed matching engine deterministically rebuild its exact in-memory state.

blocks.text: A trader should be able to submit a buy or sell order for a given symbol, at a given price and quantity. Orders should match against the resting order book using strict price-time priority, the best available price trades first, and ties at the same price are resolved by arrival order. A partially filled order should keep its place in the book for its remaining quantity. Every resulting trade should be published to a market data feed visible to subscribed participants.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the combination of the first two is what makes this problem genuinely hard.

blocks.alt: Strict price-time fairness, extremely low latency matching, no order ever lost, market integrity, and transparent market data

blocks.text: Strict price-time fairness means the best price always trades first, and among orders at an equal price, whoever arrived first is guaranteed to trade first, with zero exceptions, this is the entire basis of trader trust in the exchange. Extremely low latency matching means a single match decision has to complete in microseconds to low single-digit milliseconds, since traders compete on exactly this timing. No order lost means a crash can never silently drop or duplicate an order that was already accepted, a much harder bar than most systems in this project, since a lost order here is a direct, disputable financial harm. Market integrity means the matching logic itself must resist deliberate manipulation, not just be technically bug-free. And transparent market data means every participant sees the same order book depth and trade prints, differing only by ordinary network delay.

blocks.text: This design focuses on limit orders, an order that only trades at its specified price or better, since that already captures the core matching problem; market orders are a straightforward variant covered briefly in section 28. Clearing and settlement, the actual transfer of money and securities after a trade, is assumed to be a separate downstream system this design hands trades off to, not something this design implements itself. Each symbol is assumed to be matched by exactly one dedicated, single-threaded matching engine instance, covered in depth in section 7.3, since this is the constraint the whole architecture is built around.

blocks.text: A real exchange might see hundreds of thousands of orders per second across all symbols combined, spread across thousands of distinct tradable symbols, each handled independently by its own matching engine. A single match decision needs to complete in microseconds to low single-digit milliseconds, an extraordinarily tight budget compared to almost every other design in this project. Every trade also fans out to potentially thousands of subscribed market data consumers, traders, algorithmic trading systems, and data vendors all watching the same feed simultaneously.

blocks.text: An order enters through the order gateway and is handed to a sequencer, which assigns it a strict position in its own symbol's order stream and durably logs it before anything else happens. The order then reaches that symbol's dedicated matching engine, an in-memory order book that attempts to match it against resting orders using price-time priority, publishing any resulting trade to a trade publisher, which feeds both the market data feed and downstream clearing and settlement.

blocks.text: Each symbol's order book holds two sides, bids, buy orders sorted with the highest price first, and asks, sell orders sorted with the lowest price first. Within each individual price level, orders are held in a first-in-first-out queue, since arrival order is exactly what breaks a tie between two orders at the same price.

blocks.text: An incoming order is matched against the best available price on the opposite side of the book first. If several resting orders share that same best price, whichever one arrived earliest matches first, and a partial fill keeps the remaining quantity of an order in its same queue position rather than moving it to the back.

blocks.text: Exactly one matching engine instance owns each symbol, and it processes that symbol's orders strictly one at a time, in arrival order. This is not an implementation convenience, it is a structural requirement, splitting one symbol's order book across multiple concurrent matching threads would make the exact price-time priority guarantee itself impossible to uphold consistently.

blocks.text: Prices and quantities are stored as integers, in the smallest meaningful unit, exactly like the payment system and digital wallet designs, to avoid floating-point rounding errors in a domain where an off-by-a-fraction price could itself constitute a real, disputable trading error. The order book itself is not a database table read on every match at all, it is an in-memory structure per symbol, for the same latency reasons the digital wallet's balance check could never tolerate a slow, disk-backed read on its hot path.

After a crash, a new matching engine instance replays every logged order in its original sequence, deterministically reconstructing the exact prior order book state before resuming normal matching

blocks.text: The happy path is the match flow above, a durably logged order matched against the book in strict price-time order, with any resulting trade published outward. The workflow worth walking through separately is crash recovery, since the matching engine's authoritative state lives in memory for speed, a crash would ordinarily mean losing the entire order book. Because every order was durably logged before it was ever matched, a fresh instance can simply replay that log from the beginning, in the exact original sequence, and arrive at the identical order book state the crashed instance had, before accepting a single new order.

blocks.alt: An incoming order is routed by its symbol to that symbol's own dedicated matching engine, never split across engines for the same symbol

blocks.text: This is a sharper partitioning rule than anywhere else in this project, it is not merely a performance optimization, sending two orders for the same symbol to two different engines would make consistent price-time priority for that symbol impossible to guarantee at all.

blocks.alt: A single symbol's engine falling behind is addressed by optimizing that engine's own code path, since it fundamentally cannot be parallelized; overall throughput instead scales by simply running more symbols, each on its own independent engine

blocks.text: This is the sharpest scaling contrast in the whole project: every other design scaled a hot spot by adding more parallel workers behind it, here, one symbol's matching throughput has a hard, structural ceiling, and total system throughput instead comes from the sheer number of symbols running independently side by side.

from collections import deque
from enum import Enum
from typing import Deque, Dict, List


class Side(Enum):
    BUY = "buy"
    SELL = "sell"


# One order: which side it is on, its limit price, and how much quantity remains unfilled.
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id: str, side: Side, price: int, quantity: int):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.side = side
        self.price = price
        self.remaining_quantity = quantity


# One completed match between a buy and a sell order.
class Trade:
    def __init__(self, buy_order_id: str, sell_order_id: str, price: int, quantity: int):
        self.buy_order_id = buy_order_id
        self.sell_order_id = sell_order_id
        self.price = price
        self.quantity = quantity

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"buy={self.buy_order_id} sell={self.sell_order_id} price={self.price} qty={self.quantity}"


# A single-symbol, single-threaded order book and matching engine, enforcing
# price-time priority: best price matches first, and among equal prices,
# whichever order arrived earliest (first in the queue) matches first.
class MatchingEngine:
    def __init__(self):
        # Bids: highest price first. Asks: lowest price first. Each price level is
        # its own first-in-first-out queue, preserving arrival order for ties.
        self._bids: Dict[int, Deque[Order]] = {}
        self._asks: Dict[int, Deque[Order]] = {}
        self._orders_by_id: Dict[str, Order] = {}   # for looking up remaining quantity by id

    # Submits a new order, matching it against the opposite side of the book
    # as far as possible, and resting any unfilled remainder in the book.
    def submit(self, incoming: Order) -> List[Trade]:
        self._orders_by_id[incoming.order_id] = incoming
        trades: List[Trade] = []
        opposite_side = self._asks if incoming.side == Side.BUY else self._bids

        while incoming.remaining_quantity > 0 and opposite_side:
            best_price = min(opposite_side) if incoming.side == Side.BUY else max(opposite_side)   # best price on the opposite side

            # A buy only matches at or below its limit price; a sell only matches at or above its limit price.
            price_acceptable = (best_price <= incoming.price) if incoming.side == Side.BUY else (best_price >= incoming.price)
            if not price_acceptable:
                break   # no acceptable price left on this side; stop matching

            queue_at_level = opposite_side[best_price]
            resting = queue_at_level[0]   # earliest-arrived order at this price level: time priority

            fill_quantity = min(incoming.remaining_quantity, resting.remaining_quantity)
            incoming.remaining_quantity -= fill_quantity
            resting.remaining_quantity -= fill_quantity

            buy_order_id = incoming.order_id if incoming.side == Side.BUY else resting.order_id
            sell_order_id = resting.order_id if incoming.side == Side.BUY else incoming.order_id
            trades.append(Trade(buy_order_id, sell_order_id, best_price, fill_quantity))   # trade executes at the RESTING order's price

            if resting.remaining_quantity == 0:
                queue_at_level.popleft()   # fully filled; remove from the front of the queue
                if not queue_at_level:
                    del opposite_side[best_price]   # no orders left at this price level at all

        if incoming.remaining_quantity > 0:
            # Unfilled remainder rests in the book, at the back of its own price level's queue.
            same_side = self._bids if incoming.side == Side.BUY else self._asks
            same_side.setdefault(incoming.price, deque()).append(incoming)

        return trades

    def remaining_quantity(self, order_id: str) -> int:
        order = self._orders_by_id.get(order_id)
        return 0 if order is None else order.remaining_quantity


if __name__ == "__main__":
    engine = MatchingEngine()

    # Two resting sell orders at different prices; S1 submitted before S2.
    engine.submit(Order("S1", Side.SELL, 50, 100))
    engine.submit(Order("S2", Side.SELL, 49, 50))

    # A buy order for 120 shares at 50: should match the better price (49) first, then 50.
    trades1 = engine.submit(Order("B1", Side.BUY, 50, 120))
    print("Trades from B1 (expects price priority, then a partial fill):")
    for t in trades1:
        print(f"  {t}")
    print(f"Remaining resting quantity for S1 at price 50: {engine.remaining_quantity('S1')}")

    # A third sell order at the same price as S1's remainder, submitted after it.
    engine.submit(Order("S3", Side.SELL, 50, 20))

    # A buy order for 40 shares at 50: should match S1's remainder FIRST (time priority), then S3.
    trades2 = engine.submit(Order("B2", Side.BUY, 50, 40))
    print("Trades from B2 (expects time priority: S1's remainder before S3):")
    for t in trades2:
        print(f"  {t}")
    print(f"Remaining resting quantity for S3 at price 50: {engine.remaining_quantity('S3')}")
    print(f"S1 fully filled and removed from the book: {str(engine.remaining_quantity('S1') == 0).lower()}")

items: Architecture: a durably sequenced, per-symbol single-threaded matching engine over an in-memory price-time-priority order book, feeding a market data feed and downstream clearing and settlement.
Capacity: hundreds of thousands of orders per second across thousands of independently matched symbols, at microsecond to low-single-digit-millisecond match latency.
The core techniques: a price-time-priority order book and matching algorithm, and a write-ahead log enabling deterministic crash recovery, both worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: a symbol-partitioned, append-only write-ahead log as the durability mechanism behind an otherwise entirely in-memory matching engine.
End-to-end workflows: a normal match flow and a crash recovery flow via log replay, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strictly ordered, strongly consistent matching engine per symbol, paired with an eventually consistent, network-delayed external market data view.

Trade-offs: one single-threaded engine per symbol versus multiple threads sharing one symbol's book versus a single engine for all symbols, compared directly on the fairness guarantee and throughput ceiling each provides.
